content:
Greg ran when he was afraid.

I learned this on a Tuesday afternoon, when he stopped answering messages after a disagreement about the future.

The disagreement had begun with a question about the van. I had asked whether he would ever consider selling it and moving into a real house. He had turned the question into a joke. I had asked again. He had gone quiet.

“I’m not asking you to give up your life,” I said.

“It’s not a life. It’s a van.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Do I?”

The tone sharpened.

“I want to know whether you can imagine a future that isn’t built around leaving,” I said.

Greg had looked away.

That was when I knew the question had reached somewhere real.

“I need time,” he said.

“Time to think or time to disappear?”

He flinched.

“That was unfair,” I admitted.

“It was accurate.”

Then he left.

At first, I assumed he was taking a walk. Then an hour passed. Then two. His phone went to voicemail. The van was gone from the curb.

I sat in the studio with the lights off and tried not to build a story from the silence.

He had left me. He had gotten tired. He had decided that love was easier when it stayed inside songs.

By evening, the story had become unbearable.

I went to the car wash. The doors were locked. The community center was dark. Mara was not home. I walked to the overlook and stood beneath the trees, staring at the road.

The van appeared after midnight.

Greg parked without turning off the engine. He climbed out and closed the door. His hair was windblown, his face exhausted.

“You’re angry,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You have every right.”

“That doesn’t fix it.”

“No.”

I crossed my arms. “Where were you?”

“Driving.”

“For ten hours?”

“I stopped twice.”

“Did you tell me?”

“No.”

“Did you think about telling me?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“I didn’t.”

The honesty did not make the answer easier.

“You don’t get to vanish because a question scares you,” I said.

“I know.”

“You don’t get to make me sit in an empty room and guess whether I still have a relationship.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you?”

Greg looked toward the road. “Because I thought if I left before you asked me to change, I could decide that the ending was mine.”

The anger shifted into something more painful.

“I wasn’t asking you to stop being yourself,” I said.

“I know.”

“I was asking whether there was room for me in the future.”

“I know.”

“You keep saying you know.”

“Because I do now.”

I looked at him. “What did you figure out on the road?”

He rubbed a hand over his face. “I don’t know how to be asked to stay without hearing it as a demand to become someone else.”

“And I don’t know how to ask for a future without hearing your silence as rejection.”

“That’s a bad combination.”

“It is.”

The night wind moved between us.

Greg stepped closer. “I’m sorry.”

“I know.”

“No. I need to say it better. I’m sorry I made my fear your problem. I’m sorry I left without telling you. I’m sorry I used distance to avoid a conversation I was supposed to have with you.”

My eyes burned.

“I’m sorry I made it sound like you were failing because you wanted your life to stay recognizable,” I said. “I love the van. I love the way you make a home out of things other people overlook. I just need to know whether the home has room for me.”

Greg's face crumpled into tenderness.

“It does,” he said.

“How do you know?”

“Because when I drove away, every road looked wrong without you in the passenger seat.”

I wanted to forgive him immediately. The wanting was not enough.

“That’s romantic,” I said. “It’s not a plan.”

“You’re right.”

He pulled a folded paper from his pocket. It was a receipt covered in handwriting.

“I stopped at a diner and made a list,” he said. “Not a very good one.”

I took it.

The list held small ideas. A better mattress. A second key. A savings account for repairs and emergencies. A way to spend part of each month in one place without treating the van like a prison. A promise to answer the phone when he needed space.

At the bottom, in larger letters, he had written: ASK, DO NOT RUN.

I looked up.

“I don’t need you to solve everything tonight,” I said.

“Good. I’m very tired.”

“I need you to come home.”

“I’m here.”

“I need you to stay long enough to talk tomorrow.”

“I can do that.”

I moved closer. “I need to know you’ll tell me before you leave next time.”

“I will.”

“And if you don’t?”

“You get to be angry. You get to leave. You get to decide what you can live with.”

The answer was not a guarantee. It was accountability.

I touched his cheek. “Can I kiss you?”

His eyes closed beneath my hand. “Yes.”

The kiss was not an eraser. It was an acknowledgment that love could survive a mistake without pretending the mistake had not happened.

Greg held me carefully. When I pulled away, he kept his forehead against mine.

“I love you,” he said.

“I love you too.”

“I’m going to say that before I do something stupid.”

“You should try saying it before you drive for ten hours.”

“That’s more advanced.”

I laughed against his mouth.

The van was still parked beneath the trees. The road was still open behind it. Nothing had become magically safe.

But Greg had come back.

This time, he stayed.

The next day, Greg returned to the overlook with a notebook. He sat beneath the trees and wrote down the time he had left, the places he had stopped, and the moments when he could have called but did not.

“You are documenting your crimes,” I said.

“I am documenting my patterns.”

“That sounds less dramatic.”

“I can call it a crime if it helps me remember.”

I sat beside him. “What do you want to do with the list?”

“Show it to my therapist.”

“Good.”

“And to you, if you want.”

“I want the plan, not the punishment.”

Greg nodded. “Then the plan is: when I need space, I say where I am going and when I will contact you. If I cannot talk, I send a message. If I break the plan, I tell you what happened instead of pretending it did not.”

“And if I panic?”

“You tell me you are panicking, not that I am evil.”

“That is a high standard.”

“I am willing to be ambitious.”

I leaned into him. “I will try.”

“Honestly?”

“Honestly.”

He reached for my hand. The notebook lay open between us, the paper fluttering in the wind.

“I don’t want to become the person who makes you monitor every silence,” Greg said.

“Then keep coming back before silence becomes a story.”

“I will.”

“And I will tell you when I need reassurance.”

“I will give it without making you apologize for needing it.”

The agreement was small. It did not guarantee perfection. It gave the future a direction.

Greg closed the notebook and put it away.

“Can I kiss you?” he asked.

“You can.”

He kissed me beneath the trees. The road remained open behind the van, but neither of us needed to take it that day.

When I returned to Beach City, Greg put the notebook in a drawer beside the new key.

“You are not going to hide it?” I asked.

“No. But I am not going to make it the center of our home.”

“Good.”

He opened the drawer again. “Would you like to add anything?”

I wrote one line beneath his: ASK BEFORE ASSUMING THE DOOR IS CLOSED FOREVER.

Greg read it twice.

“That is a good rule,” he said.

“It is a difficult one.”

“Most good rules are.”

We closed the drawer together.

Greg did not open it again that night. Instead, he made dinner and let me choose the music.

I chose something loud. He complained. I danced while he cooked.

“You are distracting the chef,” he said.

“The chef is very resilient.”

“The chef is making soup.”

“The soup will survive.”

He turned from the stove and kissed me. The argument became a memory before it could become a wall.

Later, the notebook stayed closed in the drawer, and both of us slept.

In the morning, Greg opened the drawer only long enough to place the new key beside the notebook.

The two objects rested together without competing.

I made coffee. He made pancakes.

neither of us ran.

The road remained available, but home was closer.

We sat together on the couch until the light changed. Greg played a melody with one hand while I rested against his shoulder.

It was enough.

For now.

That was sufficient.

The plan could wait.
